institutionName: Hong Kong University of Science and Technology

questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Personal connection to the destination (heritage / friends there/ etc.)

questions.question: Please explain: *
Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: English speaking country, A top ranking university, Close to where I have family (in Asia)

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: We received a lot of information up front by the international office of HKUST. It was a lot to go through with every email, but it worked.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: We had 3 days of orientation, which included a small campus tour, an organized trip to IKEA to purchase things for the dorm etc., a welcome dinner with all exchange students, and a voluntary day tour (two options) where you can explore Hong Kong (the tour had to be paid in advance).

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer: The only available option was either on campus housing that I chose, which were undergraduate halls (even though I am a Master student). There were 9 available halls at the time I was there, and 2 more in the process of being built. Even if you opt to have your own housing you have to pay for the dormitory. The second option was off campus housing which is called Jockey Club Hall and you have to take a bus ride from there to campus, so it's a bit less convenient.

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer: The dormitory does have a kitchen area but it is NOT equipped with a stove. There is a water fountain and a microwave. Some people bought an electric stove to cook and kitchen utensils (also not provided), but I chose to eat in the canteens on campus, which worked out well. One meal for me was usually around 30HKD - 55 HKD. There are multiple canteens to choose from, as well as small chain restaurants where students eat on campus.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
questions.answer: Most of the dormitories are old to be honest and you are always in a shared room meaning you will have a roommate that you cannot choose yourself and will not get any information on until you meet in person. There is a period in the beginning where you are able to switch rooms but you already need to know to which room you want to switch to. The better dormitories are Hall 6 and upwards. Some dorms have shared bathrooms which are not very nice, but it all depends on the hall you get (in some halls you only share the bathroom with one other room). I found living on campus more convenient, it's also usually BA exchange students who opt for it. Master level exchange students tend to opt for the off campus housing.

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I would have appreciated it if we were able to make some indications in terms of compatibility with the roommate. For example a simple survey asking for the sleeping habits and waking times would have been beneficial to ensure you have a similar rhythm as your roommate.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: There were many links to navigate and things to do even before arriving in Hong Kong, and I found the process difficult and not easily understandable. It worked out in the end but I needed a lot of time to familiarize myself with it, even though there were websites explaining it.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: During August we already had to plan out our courses that we are interested in and use a website  where you see if the courses clash time-wise. Then you get a time slot from when you are able to register for courses. This differs per person. It's hectic because it usually coincides with the time when exchange students are arriving in Hong Kong so make sure to have time for that. You get waitlisted for most courses in my experience and then have two weeks (so called add/drop period) where you get to finalize your choices. Definitely already attend the classes you want to take even though you might not be enrolled yet.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: The international office and the office of academic registry send you emails and informs you of deadlines.  The shopping cart tool is also helpful, as well as the timetable planner (both are from HKUST) to map out the courses you're interested in.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got into all of the classes I wanted, but for some of them I was on the waitlist and they had to manually add me because the class capacity was full.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: If you approach the prof in the add/drop period and ask to let you join, it most often works. Also even if that period is open there will still be a chance to change courses if you have valid reasons for it. Ask the department that you were allocated to for help.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: Both

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I had 4 courses in total - 3 were BA level and 1 was MA level. I was informed when applying that most courses I am able to take would be BA level due to HKUST regulations on that, but I was able to enroll into one MA level courses.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: There are more forms of assessment throughout the semester, and the semester itself is shorter (beginning of September until mid December).

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: Data Visualizations, Data Mining, Cloud Computing and Big Data Systems, Fundamentals of AI

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your second semester. *
What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I really enjoyed the course Data Visualizations (COMP6411D) and would recommend taking that.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: There were some sports clubs like volleyball, soccer, track & field etc. and there are two small gyms. The Shaw Auditorium has a few cultural events and performances which are free for students. And there are clubs on campus that you can join for social activities, e.g. a club for arts, various sports clubs, etc.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I would recommend to go travelling if you can and to explore the lesser known neighbourhoods in HK.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: A trip to Shenzen is easy and fast since it borders HK. I highly recommend going to Guangzhou for a weekend trip!

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: It was okay to adjust, but in my experience you will stay in your exchange bubble anyway. Of course try to interact with local people too.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: The language barrier was a bit tougher than I expected. Even though all students are able to speak English too, it seems that a lot of full time local students feel more comfortable with Cantonese and already have their friend groups, so they are less open to talking to exchangers.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The food

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1. Share a taxi to campus with other people arriving around the same time (get in touch via Whatsapp etc beforehand). This way you already get to know people and also share the costs.
2. Get an octopus card on campus at 7eleven and top it off with cash (it only works with cash so make sure you already have that sorted). There are also ways to have it digitally.
3. Bring your own bedding if you have space for it, otherwise you can also get it second hand at the "adopt don't shop" campaign during orientation or at IKEA

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: There are two ATM machines on campus, the right one at least doesn't have an additional fee for when I withdrew money.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Being able to travel within Asia and visit friends and family of mine.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Connecting with other people on a deeper level and living with a roommate.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
